source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Fifteen LLMs do worse when the task is revealed over several turns than when it is given at once. Most of the loss is unreliability, not lost skill. Early wrong assumptions are not recovered.
numbers: Average drop 39% over six generation tasks (-35% in the 15-model main figure); aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%; N=10 simulations per model and condition, over 200,000 conversations, T=1. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) degrade the same way; their replies are 33% longer on average and carry more assumptions.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Tasks are code, SQL, API calls, math, data-to-text, summaries; no hardware. The user is simulated. Sharded instructions are not the same as a human reporting measurements.
agent_relevance: Bears on gap 8: long test-and-report loops are a weak spot of chat LLMs. Do not let the agent commit to a cause early; keep an explicit hypothesis list and state summary.

source: Laban et al. (2025) Lost in Conversation: RECAP and SNOWBALL mitigation
finding: Restating all previous information helps but does not close the gap. Lowering the assistant temperature does not fix multi-turn unreliability.
numbers: RECAP (final-turn restatement) and SNOWBALL (restate at every turn) beat SHARDED but still lag FULL and CONCAT on GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. Temperature grid for assistant and user in {1.0,0.5,0.0}: unreliability stays high even at 0.
limits: RECAP assumes you know the last turn, which is unrealistic. Only two models tested. No test of a running state summary written by the model itself.
agent_relevance: A running state summary (what is measured, what is ruled out) is a cheap partial fix; expect a partial gain, not a cure. Supports an explicit state register over free chat history.

source: Santos and Becker (2024) Not the Silver Bullet: LLM-enhanced programming error messages are ineffective in practice
finding: In a controlled within-subjects study, GPT-4 explanations of compiler errors beat stock compiler messages on time-to-fix in only 1 of 6 tasks. Expert handwritten messages did better.
numbers: N=106 students (113 recruited), six buggy C programs, each randomly given stock GCC, handwritten or GPT-4 message; 10-minute cap per task; 98% of attempts fixed.
limits: Novice software debugging with error messages, not hardware, not open chat. Single class at one university. A compiler message is a one-shot aid.
agent_relevance: Closest controlled time-to-fix design to gap 3. Shows strong benchmark results can vanish with real users. Expect small or null time effects for chat help in hardware until measured.

source: Evaluating Generative AI as a Real-Time Troubleshooting Assistant in Practical Electronics Training (2026 preprint)
finding: Per a search summary: a quasi-experiment in basic vocational electronics (AI-assisted group vs traditional control, pre and post tests) found AI useful for procedural questions but no clear fall in technical assembly errors.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not read: the page returned HTTP 403.
limits: Not opened. Preprint, not peer reviewed; quasi-experimental per the summary. A pointer, not evidence.
agent_relevance: The only controlled-ish bench study found; gap 3 stays largely open. Get the PDF by another route before citing numbers.

source: Rahman, Hasan, Ahmed, Sultana (2026) Evaluating LLMs' Effectiveness on Real-World Consumer Device Repair Questions
finding: On 991 real repair questions with technician reference answers, six LLMs give useful but unreliable advice. Phone repair is worst and least safe. Errors cluster on board-level diagnosis and skipped continuity tests.
numbers: 991 questions (Reddit; phone, computer, data recovery), six models, English and Bangla, LLM judge. GPT-5.4 best: 0.84 on English data recovery; safety 0.88 English and 0.76 Bangla for computer repair. Claude 4.6, Gemini 3.1 and Qwen 3.6 score below 0.25 on safety for phone repair in both languages. Higher completeness did not mean safer advice.
limits: Text questions only (image-dependent posts were removed). LLM judge scored the answers. Figures read from text; chart values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit physical-check step: models skip continuity and measurement steps and prefer software fixes. Score safety and correctness separately in agent tests.

source: OmniSch authors (2026) PCB schematic benchmark, arXiv 2604.00270
finding: Large multimodal models find symbols in real schematics only moderately well and almost cannot rebuild the connections. Telling the model where a symbol is raises its score a lot.
numbers: 1,854 real schematics. Symbol F1: Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.66, Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.59, Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.59, GPT-5.2 0.53, human engineer 0.97. Best net detection F1 27.44%, net-name accuracy 25.07%. Agentic search with ground-truth box: GPT-5.2 symbol F1 0.69 to 0.86, Claude 0.51 to 0.80. Removing text raised Claude F1 0.62 to 0.72.
limits: Drawn schematics, not bench photos. No hallucination rate; error analysis is qualitative. Text and table model lists do not match.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no per-image false-claim rate, but connectivity reading is far below human. Breadboard photos are probably harder. Locate-then-verify aids help, which fits a verify-before-accept step.

source: AMSbench (2025) benchmark of MLLMs on analog and mixed-signal circuits, arXiv 2505.24138
finding: Perception drops with circuit size. Component counting collapses on hard circuits. Models name elements better than they read topology.
numbers: Eight models. Total-count accuracy easy to hard: Gemini 0.88 to 0.45, GPT-4o 0.75 to 0.26, Claude 3.7 0.72 to 0.01. Topology NED Gemini 0.73 to 1.34. Function ID with image options: Grok-3 0.22 vs 0.77 text; Gemini 0.94 vs 0.95. Testbench Syntax@5 zero for all but GPT-4o (0.084). Best trade-off QA 0.58.
limits: Older models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7). Hallucination is described qualitatively; no rate. Some pass@k rows are non-monotonic, so some table numbers are suspect.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: image error rises with density, but still no false-claim rate with a control. Image-only input costs some models far more than others; use text-described wiring as a control arm.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Reasoning models state better-calibrated confidence than their non-reasoning twins, and the gain comes from slow-thinking behaviours (trying alternatives, backtracking).
numbers: Six reasoning models, six datasets, 36 settings: reasoning model strictly better on all calibration metrics in 33 of 36. Removing slow-thinking steps lowers calibration; prompting non-reasoning models to think slowly raises it.
limits: Abstract page only read (models and datasets not named there). QA datasets, not diagnosis. Aggregate calibration says nothing about single wrong claims such as a 99% pin claim.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: partly yes for reasoning models, but only aggregate and on QA. The Ghosh and Panday spread (ECE 0.122 to 0.726) is not resolved. Keep evidence-based confidence in the scaffold rather than trusting stated numbers.

source: DCPO (2026) calibration degeneration under RLVR, arXiv 2603.09117
finding: Per a search summary: reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards improves reasoning but makes models over-confident on wrong answers; fixing calibration tends to cost accuracy.
limits: Not opened; snippet only. Do not cite figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: suggests newer RL-trained reasoning models may be more overconfident on wrong answers. Points the opposite way from d08; unresolved.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning for information seeking (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: Choosing the next question by simulated expected information gain beats asking whatever the model suggests, including on a troubleshooting dataset.
numbers: FloDial troubleshooting (894 dialogues, 153 faults, 20 turns), GPT-4 success rate: direct prompting 43.7%, UoT 67.3%, adapted ToT 60.3%, CoT 32.8%; mean length in successes 7.8 vs 13.4. Medical DX 91.3% to 97.0%; MedDG 72.3% to 88.0%. Average gain 38.1% over direct prompting across five datasets and models (the arXiv v3 abstract reportedly gives 57.8%).
limits: Closed set of faults, yes/no answers, non-overlapping hypotheses, simulated user. More compute than direct prompting. Direct-prompt numbers differ slightly between main and appendix tables (91.3 vs 89.4).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: yes, information-gain ordering of questions helps on appliance-style troubleshooting. Not tested for cost-weighted bench measurements or for real hardware.

source: McCabe, Lukens, Huang (2026) CoffeeBench: Can LLM agents efficiently identify appliance faults?
finding: On a simulated coffee maker, LLM agents often fail to find the fault from sensor data alone. The best models narrow the options over iterations and reach a diagnosis.
numbers: Abstract only: initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning predict success; authors suggest explicit episode-state tracking to cut timeouts and a deliberation loop to refine hypotheses. No success rates read.
limits: Abstract page only. Simulated appliance, no human in the loop.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 8: supports a state tracker plus a hypothesis-refinement loop. Early uncertainty could drive a stop-or-ask rule.

source: When LLMs sit above diagnostic tools: unrealized complementarity in industrial fault diagnosis (2026), arXiv 2610.05031
finding: An LLM given a specialist tool's prediction does better than alone but worse than the tool alone. Wrong tool labels flip some correct answers, but missed corrections are the bigger loss.
numbers: Tennessee Eastman, 150 runs, seven LLMs (1,050 rows): unaided 64.67%, with advice 77.43%, specialist alone 83.33%, oracle selector 92.76%. Of 99 rows with LLM right and tool wrong, 15 (15.2%) became wrong. Of 295 tool-only-correct rows, 47.5% (140) were missed. Bearing sets: 18 of 22 comparisons include zero.
limits: Simulated chemical plant and wafer data, not bench hardware. Model versions are 2026 names we cannot reproduce. Wafer part is exploratory (23 of 60 correct; wrong advice flipped 6).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 7 side evidence: an external check is under-used more than over-trusted. A forced measurement step must also force the agent to act on the result.

source: Caminha et al. (2025) Evaluating LLMs and prompting strategies for hardware diagnosis from textual user reports, arXiv 2507.00742
finding: On text reports, many small models name the faulty component well; chain-of-thought helps big models but few-shot is needed for output format in small ones.
numbers: FACTO: 853 reports, 8 categories, 27 open models plus gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini, 98,948 inferences. Best F1 0.767 (gpt-4o CoT), best small model gemma-2-2b 0.727, gains level off near 30B. qwen2.5-1.5b: 0.000 zero-shot vs 0.673 few-shot.
limits: Component classification from text, not a diagnosis dialogue. The conclusion says CoT+FS is best, but the table shows CoT alone best for most models.
agent_relevance: Triage from text is not the hard part. The hard part is image and measurement handling (gaps 1, 2).

source: Benchmarking LLMs for Verilog design flows (2026), arXiv 2607.22759
finding: A refine loop of up to 5 iterations with compiler and testbench feedback gives only small gains with small open models. No split by verifier type is reported.
numbers: 50 tasks (23 combinational, 14 sequential, 8 FSM, 5 mixed). Adding the loop: syntax 63.3% to 67.8%, sim pass 46.1% to 48.9%. Final: sim pass 51.8%. TinyLlama-1.1B 60.7%, Llama-3-8B 59.3%, StarCoder2-7B 35.3%. Text says generation time fell 46% (8.84 s to 4.77 s) but the table shows 5.11 s.
limits: Tiny benchmark, small models, three runs; numbers inconsistent inside the paper. No tokens or cost. Does not separate compiler feedback from waveform analysis.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no clean answer here. Weak evidence that feedback loops give small gains at small scale.

source: AutoVeriFix+ (2026) staged feedback for Verilog generation, arXiv 2603.11489
finding: Stage-by-stage feedback on GPT-4: the largest gain switches by benchmark. Testbench input/output feedback was largest on one set; syntax feedback on the other. Trace-aware debug added a smaller gain.
numbers: RTLLM v2.0 function pass@1: baseline 51.6, +syntax 52.4, +I/O 74.6, +trace 79.0 (gains +0.8, +22.2, +4.4). VerilogEval-Human: 43.5, 68.1, 77.2, 78.1 (gains +24.6, +9.1, +0.9). False positives 28.4% to 2.0% with concolic refinement on RTLLM v2.0.
limits: One model (GPT-4), fixed stage order, so gains are not shown to be additive in other orders. No reference-model ablation, no token counts, so gain per token cannot be computed.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: gains stack in order but the biggest verifier depends on the benchmark. Cheapest-first (compile, then testbench I/O) is supported; waveform trace adds about 1-4 points.

source: Check of citations of Hu and Ash (2026) and the WIP companion via Semantic Scholar API
